title: Evergreen forest gain explained about 3% (upper bound 20%) of the post-1997 runoff deficit in 121 southern eastern US basins; recorded land-cover change predicts more runoff (NLCD 1985-2024)
abstract: Question: after 1997, runoff in eastern US CAMELS basins fell below 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relations. After monthly rain and temperature terms, a deficit of -35 mm/yr (water years 2010-2025) remains south of 39 N, 70% of it in November-April (bundle f3ac8247). Paired-catchment experiments show that conversion of hardwood forest to pine cuts water yield, mostly in the dormant season. Did evergreen forest gain, or other recorded land-cover change, cause the deficit? Approach: a plan fixed before data extraction. We counted Annual NLCD Collection 1.2 classes at 30 m in 244 basins (121 south of 39 N) for 19 map years 1985-2024 and related changes to model residuals by cross-section, a physical bound with the paired-catchment effect of -1 to -4 mm/yr per percentage point (pp), a within-basin panel with basin and year effects, and GIMMS winter leaf area. Intervals are 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals. Results: southern evergreen cover rose only 0.49 pp. The basin response agreed with paired catchments (cross-section -1.9 mm/yr per pp, CI -6.3 to +1.6; all basins -4.0, -8.5 to -0.8; panel -2.5 and -4.0), winter LAI followed NLCD evergreen change (rho 0.35-0.53) and recent harvest raised runoff (+4.9 mm/yr per pp). But evergreen gain explains about 3% of the deficit (fitted share 0.03, CI -0.08 to 0.14; physical bound 0.03-0.06, upper CI 0.21), which meets the planned rule for 'cannot explain'. All recorded land-cover change implies +5 to +7 mm/yr more runoff, not less. Basins with stable cover lost -29 mm/yr (CI -46 to -13; dormant -24). Conclusion: land-cover class change does not cause the southern eastern US runoff deficit; changes inside forests (ageing, species shift), seasonal soil-water storage or climate-input effects remain. Limitations: NLCD starts in 1985 and does not record forest structure; basins are reference basins; the northern slope is confounded by region.
